sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur, and even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction, and evaluate the resulting supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the tested prompt transformations produce a reproducible redistribution profile on these excluded variants. We then separate recurring representation change from signed readout contribution and decision failure. For a fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. RSS therefore provides a way to identify recurring sparse representation changes and quantify their contribution to a downstream readout without equating representation change with failure. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense language model activations into sparse features intended to separate signals entangled by superposition (Elhage et al., 2022; Huben et al., 2024). Related inputs can change which features respond, including shifts toward more specific features and changes under prompt or surface form variation (Chanin et al., 2025; Cho & Hockenmaier, 2025; Verma et al., 2026). Such prompt variations can also affect model behavior (Sclar et al., 2024; Mizrahi et al., 2024). Using SAE features to characterize this variation requires distinguishing responses specific to individual inputs from patterns that recur across related inputs, and assessing their relevance to downstream computation. Tracking one feature can reveal its response while missing changes elsewhere, whereas aggregate activation distances summarize overall change without identifying the contributing features. We refer to changes in how activity is distributed across the sparse basis as representation redistribution. Observing redistribution on one set of inputs does not establish which feature changes recur beyond those observations, and recurrence alone does not show whether the same changes matter to downstream computation. We therefore study recurring redistribution as distinct object, asking which sparse feature changes repeat across related prompt transformations and persist beyond the variants used to identify them. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which combines response magnitude with recurrence and directional consistency to select responsive support. Features and their directions are selected on one set of variants and then held fixed when evaluating disjoint variants. MeanRSS summarizes the response magnitude of the selected support (Figure 1). 1 Figure 1: RSS under prompt transformations. In the illustrated five-variant selection, boxed features change in the same direction in at least four variants. MeanRSS averages their absolute response magnitudes. Recurring representation change is not the same as downstream effect. selected feature can receive little readout weight, contributions from different features can cancel, and change in readout score need not cross the decision threshold. We therefore decompose the contribution of recurrent changes to fixed linear readout and assess the remaining margin relative to the clean input. We evaluate this connection through offline audits of two frozen safety readouts with known labels. Our main contributions are as follows. We introduce RSS to identify sparse feature changes that recur in consistent direction across related prompt transformations, and evaluate fixed supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs, the tested transformations yield reproducible redistribution profile beyond the variants used to select the supports. We separate recurring representation change from downstream contribution and decision failure. For fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout weight, directional alignment, and the clean margin connect recurrent changes to readout effects and threshold crossing. We show that recurrent changes selected without readout information nevertheless explain substantial held out readout variation. In two frozen safety readouts, RSS supports reconstruct held out logit changes and retain offline audit utility when combined with the clean margin. Median supports of 20 and 19 features yield recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958, versus 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Sparse autoencoder features have been evaluated through reconstruction, sparsity, and downstream use (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Makelov et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025; Kantamneni et al., 2025). Related inputs can also alter which features respond, including absorption into more specific features and changes under prompt or surface form variation (Chanin et al., 2025; Cho & Hockenmaier, 2025; Verma et al., 2026). Feature sensitivity has also been measured as activation reliability across semantically related texts (Tian et al., 2025). RSS instead asks which transformation induced feature changes recur after the support is fixed and evaluates those changes on variants excluded from selection. Prompt sensitivity studies show that format, ordering, and wording can alter model behavior (Zhao et al., 2021; Sclar et al., 2024; Mizrahi et al., 2024; Chatterjee et al., 2024), while other work studies stable representation directions and SAE responses to optimized pertur2 bations (Dasgupta et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). We use controlled prompt variation to study recurring redistribution within the sparse basis rather than behavioral sensitivity alone. Linear probes on SAE activations test whether task relevant information can be recovered from internal representations (Kantamneni et al., 2025), while feature interventions can reveal context dependent downstream effects (Hoang et al., 2026). Our fixed readout analysis serves different purpose. We hold the fitted readout fixed and measure how much of its prompt induced change is carried by features selected without readout information.

sections.title: 4 Experiments and Results
sections.content: 4.1 Systematic and Persistent Redistribution Across Pretrained SAEs We first test whether the tested transformations produce reproducible redistribution profile across pretrained SAEs. The study uses 1,000 English prompts across 12 content categories, generated once and fixed before SAE inference. The six settings contrast context and wrapper transformations, which alter surrounding material or presentation, with punctuation and lexical edits that modify the preserved request locally. We evaluate 27 pretrained SAEs spanning GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), Gemma 2 (Gemma Team, 2024), Gemma 3 (Gemma Team, 2025), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023), and Llama 3.1 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) across multiple layers. We normalize the six MeanRSS setting means within each SAE to compare transformation profiles rather than absolute response scales. Each setting uses five operators with three realizations each; mean changes within each operator supply the selector observations, and the evaluated token remains aligned to the preserved target span. Supplementary Section S3 and Table S3 give the full protocol, selector parameters, and SAE specifications. 5 Figure 2: Normalized MeanRSS across six prompt transformations and 27 pretrained SAEs. Each SAEs six setting means are divided by their average, so the plot compares transformation profiles rather than absolute activation scales. Large outlined diamonds show averages across SAEs. The normalized context and wrapper mean exceeds the local edit mean in all 27 SAEs, with an average difference of 0.874 and 95% interval of [0.867, 0.881] from bootstrap resampling of base prompts with the SAE panel fixed. The pattern also holds across prompts: after aggregation across SAEs, the context and wrapper mean exceeds the local edit mean for all 1,000 prompts, and every context or wrapper setting exceeds both local edits for 997. Supplementary Section S4 reports support organization and robustness to feature scaling and unavailable cases. Across four intensity levels, the median prompt level Spearman correlations between intensity and MeanRSS are 0.95 for punctuation edits, 0.74 for irrelevant context, and 0.50 for the format wrapper. Supports are selected separately at each intensity, so this tests magnitude calibration rather than persistence of the same features. Supplementary Table S12 gives the intensity definitions. We next test persistence beyond selection at two levels: whether fixed support preserves the transformation profile on held out variants, and whether its features preserve their selected directions. Figure 3 evaluates the first question. RSS gives stronger context and wrapper versus local edit separation than each comparison method in 2426 of 27 SAEs and gives the largest contrast in 22. The profile also remains stable under disjoint realization and operator holdouts (Supplementary Section S4). Directional consistency on the selection observations, including the finite sample guarantee in Proposition 2, does not guarantee the same direction on new variants. On held out variants, the response rate in the selected direction is 0.952 for RSS and 0.758 for random supports matched in size and candidate pool (Supplementary Tables S16S17). 4.2 Feature Persistence and Functional Relevance in Frozen Readouts To test whether recurring responses also affect downstream computation, we audit two frozen linear safety readouts. The functional study uses 1,800 balanced WildGuardMix prompts (Han et al., 2024), split 1,200/300/300 into training, validation, and test sets. sections.title: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: The results establish recurring redistribution as distinct property of sparse representations under prompt variation. Rather than asking only whether an individual feature responds or how far the representation moves in aggregate, RSS identifies sparse changes that recur across related transformations and remain observable on variants excluded from selection. The shared profile across pretrained SAEs further shows that these recurring changes can form structured patterns within fixed sparse basis. second implication is that recurring representation change and downstream effect are related but distinct quantities. recurrent feature response affects fixed readout through its response magnitude, readout weight, directional alignment, and the clean margin. This decomposition turns re9 Figure 6: Utility of RSS supports selected for each prompt and transformation within the frozen readout. A, R2 for reconstructed held out logit changes. B, readout errors reversed by restoring selected feature values. CD, errors and harmful false negatives captured at 20% offline review budget using known labels. Error bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. distribution from representational observation into quantity that can be related directly to downstream computation, while explaining why large changes need not cause failure and smaller aligned changes can matter near decision boundary. Most importantly, the recurring changes are selected without readout information, yet they explain substantial part of held out readout variation. Their value therefore extends beyond describing representation change: the same supports retain meaningful contribution, reconstruct logit changes, and localize changes that can alter readout decisions. This provides direct bridge from recurrent sparse representation change to functional consequence within fixed downstream computation. The results concern the tested transformations and frozen linear readouts, with the main functional holdout using new realizations of the same operators. Within this setting, RSS identifies recurring changes first and evaluates their downstream relevance separately.

sections.content: The four larger base models, which contribute twelve of these SAEs, use bfloat16 precision without quantization, while their SAEs use float32. Checkpoint preprocessing is unchanged. Gemma 3 4B and Gemma 2 2B use none, Mistral uses per token constant norm rescaling, and Llama Scope uses checkpoint specific rescaling using dataset statistics. sections.content: The 1,000 clean prompts are generated once, before any SAE inference, using GPT-5.4 snapshot gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 at temperature 0.6 with fixed acceptance criteria for length (530 words), naturalness, plausibility, category match, and duplication against previously generated prompts. Irrelevant context prepends topically unrelated benign material. Distractor context prepends benign competing task while retaining the original request as operative. Metalinguistic wrappers alter response mode or presentation. Format wrappers place the request in structured envelopes. Punctuation noise inserts local punctuation without changing the lexical sequence. Typed lexical substitution replaces noncritical words from fixed type compatible pool. The preserved target phrase appears exactly once in every valid variant. Target Token Alignment Every prompt records the character span of the preserved target. For each clean prompt and variant, the evaluated position is the final non special token overlapping that span. Prefixes and wrappers can shift the token index, but the evaluated surface span remains fixed. No mapping failures are observed across all 90,000 cases in the five-variant analysis. We compare MeanRSS sampling with uniform sampling under the same augmentation budget, rather than infer training benefit from the frozen audit. Every augmented probe uses 1,200 clean examples and 6,000 transformed examples, corresponding to five transformed examples per training prompt. The MeanRSS method samples prompt and transformation pairs according to MeanRSS computed from the training prompts, with exponent γ = 2. The uniform method samples from the same pool with equal probability. Scaling statistics and feature masks remain those of the clean probe. Figure S9 and Table S32 report the results.
